title: Springboks v Barbarians: Five takeaways as Rassie Erasmus experiments have mixed success - Planet Rugby
content: Springboks head coach Rassie Erasmus and wing Cheslin Kolbe. Following an 80-31 victory for the Springboks over the Barbarians on Saturday, here’s our five takeaways from the clash at the Nelson Mandela Bay Stadium. The Springboks overcame a slack six minutes to dominate the Barbarians in the second period and open their international season with a dominant victory. In typical Baa-Baas style, there was plenty of free-flowing rugby – from both sides – but South Africa’s success came from them doubling down on their super strengths, namely their scrum and maul. Rassie Erasmus’ men played some excellent rugby early on, going 35-7 in front thanks to Edwill van der Merwe’s double and further tries from Pieter-Steph du Toit, Jasper Wiese and Riley Norton – three of those coming after TJ Perenara and Miracle Fai’ilagi had been sin-binned. However, a yellow card of their own for Grant Williams enabled the invitational team to hit back with Franco Molina, Andrew Kellaway and Perenara adding to Virimi Vakatawa’s earlier try to reduce the arrears. That was as good as it got for the visitors, whose week on the lash caught up with them in the second period. Cheslin Kolbe crossed the whitewash at the end of the first half and they then proceeded to score 40 more points after the break. Van der Merwe completed his hat-trick while JJ Kotze, Faf de Klerk, Jesse Kriel, Andre Esterhuizen and Zach Porthen also went over to complete the rout. Erasmus will be looking for the successors to the likes of Siya Kolisi, Du Toit and perhaps even Wiese post-Rugby World Cup, but right now they remain their first choice back-row and it is easy to see why. Wiese, having spent another season in Asia in the slightly less taxing Japan Rugby League One, looked fit and sharp and was barrelling over established internationals with regularity, even at close quarters. Du Toit and Kolisi were playing slightly wider, as has often been the way since the arrival of Tony Brown, and they thrived in those spaces. It was the skipper who provided the assist for Van der Merwe’s first try with a deft pass after drawing the final defender, while his flank team-mate proved incredibly difficult to stop when probing that five-metre channel on the wing. Du Toit was also rewarded for his performance by going over the line, although it came via the more direct route with a powerful surge close to the whitewash. The trio were also among their top-tacklers, although the two-time World Rugby Player of the Year did miss a few, so there is still plenty to work on after they managed to blow off the cobwebs ahead of the England clash. The strength of the squad on Saturday may have taken a few by surprise but, as Erasmus stated, it is acting as preparation for their huge Test against the English in the Nations Championship. However, that did not prevent the Boks from trialling a few things, which included a new fly-half and second-row forward. Quan Horn, who has never started at 10 for the Lions, was handed the role in what was a fascinating move from the hosts. He has a fine passing game and a hefty left boot, and those two facets were in evidence on occasion, but his inexperience generally showed. Horn did not quite know where to stand, made a few poor decisions and ultimately needs plenty of work if he is to be comfortable going forward. Equally, he will be frustrated by his early defensive work after being run over by Alex Nankivell for Vakatawa’s score. His selection also left them without what most consider an out-and-out goal-kicker, certainly at international level, but it is a responsibility Cheslin Kolbe has taken on in Japan to great success. Kolbe has been operating at 81 per cent and the wing was handed the role against the Barbarians, where he was exceptional, kicking nine conversions. One of those kicks came after Norton touched down, the U20 captain who has yet to play a professional game for the Stormers. The youngster is very highly regarded in South Africa, and those talents were evident from the start. What was particularly noticeable was his technical work in the tight, which belied his tender years, while he did not shirk anything physically. Impressive from the lock, who looks destined to have a long Springboks career. Springboks player ratings: Cheslin Kolbe’s mixed bag, Junior Bok captain shines as Edwill van der Merwe scores three After the disappointing contest last year, neutrals were hoping for a better display in 2026 from what was, on paper at least, a talented side, but when they lost Perenara and Fai’ilagi to the sin bin and shipped three tries in that period, it did not look promising. It left them 35-7 in arrears and facing an embarrassing afternoon at the Nelson Mandela Bay Stadium, but the Boks also struggled to keep their discipline. Scrum-half Williams was yellow-carded for a deliberate knock-on, and during those 10 minutes, the Baa-Baas played some spellbinding rugby as they also touched down three times. Erasmus would have been concerned by their midfield defence with Andre Esterhuizen and Jesse Kriel biting in, giving too much space on the outside. Those two experienced centres perhaps wanted to offer a helping hand to the fly-half, who was run over by Nankivell early on, but those gaps were exploited by the invitational side at the end of the first half. However, the Barbarians were unable to maintain that momentum and a needless mistake from the restart enabled Kolbe to cross the whitewash while South Africa were down to 14 to ease the pressure going into the second period. They would then keep their foot on the throat after the break, despite an early yellow card for Aphelele Fassi. The Springboks went back to basics and were much more direct, going to their trusty maul and scrum, and duly bullied the visitors physically in the final 35 minutes. Barbarians player ratings v Springboks: ‘Incredibly annoying’ All Blacks great has flashes of brilliance as Scott Robertson’s side are ‘outclassed’ In many ways, we enjoyed TJ Perenara’s combative approach. Sometimes these games can be a bit of a jolly for those Barbarians players, but Perenara, having been given the opportunity to face South Africa for the first time since 2024, was clearly desperate to win. The former All Blacks scrum-half, to his immense credit, was everywhere both with and without the ball, but that sheer competitiveness spilled over to disrespect towards the referee. He had already been sin-binned for a high shot but, after returning to the field, Perenara did not stop moaning at the man in the middle. Morné Ferreira attempted to calm him down, warning him about his behaviour and even calling him a “legend of the game”, perhaps trying to appeal to his ego, but quite frankly he would have been better served simply penalising him and, if he continued, giving him a second yellow. Given that these games are the friendliest of friendlies, Ferreira understandably didn’t want to do that, but Perenara’s attitude was simply unacceptable and should have been sanctioned. title: France XV v England XV: Winners and losers as Les Bleus flex 'riches' in glorified training run - Planet Rugby
content: France's Nolan Le Garrec and an inset of England's George Ford. France XV beat England XV 35-19 at a sun-drenched Stade de la Rabine on Friday, a five-try evening that flattered England only in the sense that it could comfortably have been worse. Bordeaux’s rising star Marko Gazzotti was imperious at the base at eight, Nolann Le Garrec marked an emotional return to the Vannes club that made him, and an England side shorn of its first-choice spine came apart the moment the benches emptied. The lasting image was Benhard Janse van Rensburg dropping the ball over the line with nobody within ten yards of him, two days before Steve Borthwick must name a Nations Championship squad. Bordeaux’s early Top 14 exit was supposed to be the great inconvenience of France’s summer, depriving Fabien Galthie of his champions for the southern tour. On this evidence it simply handed his second string a spine of genuine quality, and Gazzotti was the heartbeat of it. The number eight carried with huge impact every time he touched the ball, linked midfield to forward play with the ease of a man who has been doing it in European finals, and gave Le Garrec a platform so clean that France’s attack purred from the first quarter. He was the best forward on the pitch by a distance, and he barely had to leave second gear to prove it. France have a problem in the back-row of their scrum only in the sense that they now have too many good options. This was Le Garrec’s night before a ball was kicked. Formed at Vannes, he had somehow never played a competitive match at La Rabine, and the emotion of hearing the Marseillaise sung back at him by the people who first watched him was written all over his face. He answered it in the perfect way, sniping over for the third try midway through the second half before departing four minutes later to a standing ovation he had earned ten years in advance. What followed showed France’s strength in the position, because Baptiste Jauneau arrived from the bench and kept the tempo exactly where his predecessor had left it. His quick tap-and-go for the fifth try, taken while all 15 England players stood admiring the scenery, was the work of a scrum-half who had read the game’s complacency long before the men in white did. For all France’s riches, the depth of their front-row has nagged at Galthie for two seasons. He will have driven home from Brittany rather happier on that score. Jefferson Poirot, recalled at 33 and six years on from walking away from international rugby, anchored the loosehead with the calm of a man who never really left, and when Régis Montagne came on around the three-quarter mark the French scrum lifted from solid to overwhelming. Throw in six uncapped players blooded without the result ever wobbling, and a coach who came to experiment leaves with a clutch of answers. The set-piece that broke England in the final quarter was assembled almost entirely from reserves. France XV v England XV: Five takeaways as Benhard Janse van Rensburg blows ‘golden chance’ as ‘error strewn’ visitors give Steve Borthwick food for thought If Gazzotti supplied the platform, Hastoy supplied the control. The fly-half was faultless off the tee in glorious kicking conditions, threaded the pass that sent Nicolas Depoortere over for the opening French try on the counter, and helped himself to a score of his own in the 51st minute that effectively closed the contest at 28-12. He managed the game with the authority of someone who knew his pack was winning the collisions, and he asked questions of England’s spacing that his opposite number never came close to asking in return. Yoram Moefana and Depoortere gave France a centre pairing of real craft and vision. Truth be known, they are probably France’s number one pairing but Galthie has so many options now. Moefana’s inside ball, a gorgeous renversement that wrong-footed the entire England line, sent Grégoire Arfeuil scorching clear for the second try and was the single most creative moment of the half. Depoortere, back in the blue of France, marked his return with the opening score and looked every inch a Test 13. England spent the night chasing shadows in the wide channels, and these two were the reason. The clearest sign of France’s depth was that their bench did not dilute the performance; it intensified it. Tixeront was central to that, thundering off the pine to add fresh legs and fresh menace to a back-row that already had England wilting. He carried hard, hunted at the breakdown and helped tip the contest from competitive to one-sided in the third quarter, the kind of cameo that turns a squad member into a tour selection. When your replacements raise the level rather than protect it, you are a side in rude health. The captain’s armband demanded a performance of control and direction, and Ford delivered flashes of the former and almost none of the latter. There were the familiar lovely touches, the odd flat pass that promised something, but for 80 minutes he could not get his backline moving or his carriers over the gainline with any rhythm. England’s most creative passages arrived in spite of their structure rather than because of it, and a fly-half of his experience leading a side this disjointed has to wear that. He set up Max Ojomoh’s late consolation, and on another night that might soften the verdict. On this one it merely underlined how little had come before it. Alex Dombrandt, Tom Curry and Ted Hill spent the evening looking like carthorses in a sweat, laboured and a yard off the pace against a French unit that moved through the gears at will. The tackle counts will flatter them, Dombrandt’s especially, but a tackle count is what you rack up when the opposition has the ball and the territory, and France had both for long stretches. Curry’s effort on his return from a grade-three calf tear was honest, yet honesty was never the problem. Breakdown speed, carry threat and the ability to live with a quicker, sharper back-row all were, and England were second best in every one of them. England XV player ratings: Cadan Murley ‘pushes his case’ for Springboks Test as Noah Caluori ‘not out of place’ The starting trio held their own early, and Asher Opoku-Fordjour did his loosehead credentials no harm. The damage came when the bench emptied. From that point England’s scrum was overpowered, shoved backwards, penalised and ultimately demoralised by a French unit running on reserves. The retreat bled into the rest of the side, concentration drained, and by the time Fabien Brau-Boirie sauntered in untouched there was not an English head still in the game. Our own ratings were generous to a fault here. A scrum that goes into reverse against a scratch French pack is not a six-out-of-ten afternoon, however willing the effort. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. The fixture was sold on a single promise, that it would be free and available to all, the modern game reaching out to its audience. The platform then spent the evening betraying that promise. Buffering at the worst possible moments, a picture that dipped to a quality you would have been embarrassed by a decade ago, and a viewing experience that turned a simple watch into a test of patience. If you make accessibility the entire pitch, the least required is a stream that holds its shape for 80 minutes. This one did not come close, and on a night when the rugby offered little, the people who tuned in for free deserved a great deal better. Here is the uncomfortable truth beneath all five tries. This was a game without a single thing riding on it, no caps, no jeopardy, no trophy, no consequence, dropped into a weekend already groaning under a URC final and the business end of the Top 14. 30-odd professionals were asked to put their bodies on the line in a contest history will not record, while the real drama of the season played out elsewhere. Janse van Rensburg’s fumble became the emblem of the whole exercise, a young man desperate to matter in a match that did not. You can dress these run-outs up as preparation, and the coaches duly did, but a glorified opposed session in front of 12,000 curious locals is a strange use of a summer Friday. The question worth asking is not how England played, it is why anyone signed this off in the first place? title: Honda's Cheapest SUV Can't Dethrone It's Best-Selling Sibling - Here's Why - CarBuzz
content: Added a section that talks about the CR-V TrailSport in more detail. Buying a Honda SUV for family needs seems like the obvious choice. They offer good reliability, practicality and comfort at a price that will not break the bank. However, in 2026, that choice may be a little confusing to make. With the HR-V and CR-V, Honda has two different propositions to offer in terms of value and practicality. So, which one makes more sense for you between the subcompact HR-V SUV vs the compact CR-V SUV? We compare their engines, exterior, interior and, finally, their price to find out which one is the better deal for you. All information has been sourced from the manufacturer or test drive experience, where available. All prices listed are MSRP, which does not include any offers or additional fees. Automakers reserve the right to update pricing at their own discretion and without notice. The Honda CR-V is available with two powertrains in the US. While the entry-level non-hybrid 1.5L is sufficient for many budget-conscious buyers, especially in the city, the hybrid system features a 1.06-kWh battery and provides more power while boosting efficiency scores throughout all trims. Both engine options are paired with a CVT gearbox. AWD is available as an option on all trims of the CR-V and CR-V Hybrid. For 2026, the powertrains get a new traction-management system for the AWD models to aid maneuverability in low-speed, low-traction situations. While neither engine option is known for its spirited driving dynamics, they are both quiet and smooth at highway speeds and offer good fuel economy in the city. There is also an option for a fuel cell EV powertrain in the CR-V e:FCEV that offers an EPA-estimated rating of 270 miles, but as that is a completely different model and does not rival the HR-V. Hence, we do not include it in this comparison. "New software tuning allows for a simulated rear differential lock at low speeds, which allows the crossover to muscle through slippery terrain if even one wheel has traction." Many have said that if the Honda HR-V has an Achilles heel, it is its engine and gearbox combination. Technically, the HR-V also has two powertrain options, one of them being hybrid. However, the US market only gets the non-hybrid option as of now. While the numbers do not seem too bad on paper, the HR-V shares its non-hybrid engine with the base Civic sedan and hatchback. This is arguably the biggest difference between the Honda CR-V and HR-V. While the engine remained the same, the surrounding chassis got heavier and larger in the shape of the subcompact SUV. As a result, the engine is adequate at city speeds, but feels strained and loud at highway speeds or while overtaking. The CVT gearbox also does not help with the added noise at constant speeds. AWD is available as an option on all trims for a premium of $1,500, much like its bigger brother, the CR-V. The Honda CR-V is bigger in almost every dimension, which results in a more traditional SUV look with a more upright stance. The HR-V is smaller, and appeals to the rising trends of crossovers and subcompact SUVs. Both cars do a good job of being inoffensive to look at, which is exactly what someone is looking for from a dependable Japanese compact SUV. While the CR-V offers multiple trims to appeal to buyers looking for either a family SUV or maybe even a rugged AWD SUV, the HR-V trims are much simpler and offer the basic, urban-focused needs of the market it serves. All-terrain tires and some tweaked cosmetics don't provide much improvement, but neither do they spoil what's already a competent crossover. The exterior on both SUVs does not massively change with each trim, except for the TrailSport trim on the CR-V Hybrid. The HR-V is smaller and will be easier to maneuver in the city or a parking space. If you live in an urban jungle, the HR-V may be better suited to you. But if you have more space to maneuver, the CR-V's bigger dimensions bode well for its interior space. Not only is the HR-V limited in its number of available trim levels, it lacks the brand's popular TrailSport variant. Buyers have flocked to Honda for its off-road oriented trim that's optional on the CR-V, Pilot, Ridgeline, and Passport models. In the CR-V's case, we can see why buyers would choose this over the HR-V's relatively simple lineup. It comes with the same hybrid powertrain as any other hybrid trim; power outputs are the same, as is its e-CVT and standard all-wheel drive. That said, this trim might sway buyers away from the HR-V for its styling and some extra standard features. It comes with standard all-terrain tires that offer improved grip off the pavement, four drive modes including Normal, Snow, Sport, and Econ, roof rails, dual exhaust, and cloth seats with orange stitching. This variant's tires lend to its slightly worse fuel economy compared to the rest of the hybrid lineup, as it gets an estimated 38/33/35 mpg. However, the rest of its design, drive modes, and tires may pull buyers away from other options. The new Honda cabin layout and simple, unlike some other manufacturers experimenting with a plethora of screens and haptic buttons in 2026. The HR-V takes inspiration from the Civic here as well, with a horizontal dashboard and physical climate controls. The honeycomb grille for the air vents adds some texture to an otherwise uneventful front cabin. So, which is bigger, CR-V or HR-V? The HR-V is noticeably smaller inside when compared to the CR-V, especially behind the front row. Adults will find the rear legroom cramped for long rides, and the trunk space is average against its subcompact SUV rivals. The CR-V received an interior tech upgrade for 2026 that makes the 9-inch touchscreen standard across all trims and brings wireless phone charging and connectivity. The dashboard follows a similar ethos of being uncluttered and as easy to use as the HR-V. The biggest difference you will see is the space behind the front row. While the shoulder room and hip room may not be considerably bigger, there is significantly more legroom. Cargo space also sees an almost 60% increase from the HR-V, to a class-leading 39.3 cu-ft expanding to 76.5 cu-ft with the seats folded. Honda has tweaked the HR-V, but base model shoppers will benefit most. Pricing is usually the most important deciding factor when picking between two cars from the same manufacturer. The entry level CR-V starts at $30,920, with prices rising up to $35,400 for the highest non-hybrid trim. The hybrid powertrains naturally demand more money, and start at $35,650 all the way till the Sport Touring Hybrid is priced at $42,550. While that is significantly more than the HR-V in any trim, the non-hybrid CR-V is pretty close in price. You do get more mileage, efficiency and power from the hybrid system. However, the interior and exterior fundamentals remain the same. There is a reason the CR-V has been a class leader in the compact SUV category, as it offers a trim for almost everybody. The HR-V is the entry-level Honda SUV model starting at $26,600. The top of the line trim starts from $30,450. It is interesting to note that the entry-level CR-V is just $470 more than the flagship HR-V trim. While you miss out on features such as leather upholstery, a moon roof, dual-zone parking climate controls and parking sensors among other quality of life features, you get a bigger SUV with a stronger engine and better economy for not much more money. The entry-level CR-V may seem spartan inside when compared to the HR-V. However, with the 2026 update of new tech features for the CR-V, that gap is closer than ever. Honda CR-V vs HR-V Sales Figures Over The Last 5 Years If we look at the sales figures over the last five years between the CR-V and HR-V, you can clearly see just how popular the former is. While the HR-V appeals to a more price-sensitive market where the sales volumes are naturally lower, the CR-V continues to dominate in the larger segment, especially after its redesign in 2023. CR-V's are also known to hold their values better, with price trends showing great stability for the model. The better option between the two compact SUVs from Honda is the CR-V. While the HR-V is cheaper, it is restricted by its engine and performance, and space for more than two people. It also does not have vastly different trims to appeal to a wider audience, something that the CR-V does so well. The price difference is marginal between the non-hybrid CR-V and HR-V, but is significantly more if you want the hybrid powertrain. The CR-V, in both its powertrain options, is a better family SUV with great interior space and reliability to keep you satisfied for many miles. We want to hear from you. title: World Cup schedule today: How to watch Netherlands v Sweden, TV channels & live stream Saturday 20 June - The Guardian
content: Live blog: the latest news from around the tournament Group F is shaping up to be one of the most competitive at the 2026 World Cup with Japan, the Netherlands and Sweden all talented enough to make a deep run. The second round of group games could reveal whether or not that is realistic. The stakes are high. Japan and the Netherlands started their World Cup campaigns by sharing the spoils, but both teams could do with a win in their second game to be sure of their place in the last 32. They may have to demonstrate more ambition than they did in their opener. Sweden, meanwhile, made a statement by putting five goals past Tunisia. Viktor Gyökeres and Alexander Isak both found the back of the net in a display that made others sit up and take note. Graham Potter’s team are worth watching. Here is your complete guide on how to watch today’s World Cup games, including kick-off times, broadcast networks and online streaming options. Ronald Koeman has faced some criticism for the changes he made when the Netherlands were leading against Japan, and many are expecting a more assertive approach against Sweden. Koeman, however, may lack the creative personnel for the Dutch to truly impose their own game. Sweden, on the other hand, demonstrated their attacking threat in a 5-1 win over Tunisia that hinted at a growing understanding between Gyökeres and Isak. If Potter can balance the forward line with the rest of his team, Sweden could be dark horses to make a run. Player to watch: Alexander Isak, Sweden – after he missed so much of his first season at Liverpool with injuries, it was refreshing to see Isak at something close to his best against Tunisia. His direct threat could trouble club teammate Virgil van Dijk. Fortune favours Kamada as Japan rescue World Cup draw with Netherlands Graham Potter: ‘I feel very Swedish when I’m working – I look a bit Swedish’ While Germany put seven goals past Curaçao in their World Cup opener, the standard of the opposition means the true gauge of Julian Nagelsmann’s team is still to be taken. The four-time winners have failed to reach the knockout stage of the last two World Cups, but they are well-placed to end that streak. In overcoming one of Conmebol’s strictest defenses in their opening match against Ecuador, Côte d’Ivoire made a statement of intent even if they needed a late winner. The Elephants have a variety of taking options that could take them far. Player to watch: Yan Diomande, Côte d’Ivoire – the in-demand RB Leipzig winger was relentless against Ecuador, showing why Liverpool and Paris Saint-Germain are reportedly interested in his services. Curaçao enjoy their moment but Havertz and ruthless Germany show no mercy ‘We are knocking on the door’: Africa’s 10 contenders target World Cup glory While Ecuador underwhelmed in their opener against Côte d’Ivoire, the team who finished an impressive second in Conmebol qualifying could still make an impact at this tournament. They must, however, show more attacking intent. Livano Comenencia’s equalizer for Curaçao against Germany was one of the moments of the World Cup so far. While his team ultimately suffered a heavy defeat, their ambition to venture forward when possible should be a warning sign to Ecuador. Player to watch: Moisés Caicedo, Ecuador – the Chelsea midfielder is Ecuador’s valve in the center of the pitch, giving them the ability to hit out on the break. Caicedo will also have to be at his creative best against Curaçao’s low block. Why Ecuador, Japan and Norway are the dark horses at this World Cup ‘Everyone is welcome with us’: Curaçao want you along for their first World Cup ride Tunisia shot themselves in the foot more than once as they opened their World Cup campaign with a 5-1 loss to Sweden – a result so poor they sacked their head coach and appointed Hervé Renard until the end of the tournament. If they can cut out the mistakes, though, they could still salvage their World Cup. Japan could be one of the most adaptable teams at this tournament if their opener against the Netherlands is anything to go by. Hajime Moriyasu knows how to set up his side to sit deep, but also to control games higher up the field. Player to watch: Takefusa Kubo, Japan – while the Real Sociedad playmaker wasn’t at his best against the Netherlands, his ability as a creator could be key to breaking down Tunisia. title: Hurricanes v Chiefs: Five takeaways as Canes enter 'greatest-ever champions' debate after All Blacks ruthlessly punish Damian McKenzie's 'disasterclass' - Planet Rugby
content: Jordie Barrett lifts the Super Rugby Pacific trophy and inset of Damian McKenzie. Following the Hurricanes’ record-breaking 60-5 victory over the Chiefs in the 2026 Super Rugby Pacific Final, here are our five takeaways. It’s been 10 years, but the Hurricanes are Super Rugby champions yet again, humiliating the Chiefs in the 2026 final to clinch just their second title. Nine tries, six conversions and a penalty goal meant that the ‘Canes racked up 60 points in what was a truly dominant thrashing of the second-best club in the tournament this year, who managed just five points in reply. A gulf in class is an understatement as the Hurricanes bossed every single facet of the game with their attack ripping the Chiefs to shreds and their defence ensuring that this one was never in doubt. Josh Moorby got the scoreboard ticking in the fifth minute, and the hosts would lead from then on with Ruben Love following eight minutes later before Fehi Fineanganofo broke the record for the most tries in a second season in the 23rd minute. Callum Harkin scored the fourth and final try of the first half with Love adding the extras and a penalty as the ‘Canes led 29-0 as the two sets of players headed to the sheds. Moorby joined Fineanganofo on 17 tries in 2026 when he crossed for the fifth try of the match just three minutes into the second half, with departing flanker Devan Flanders making it six five-pointers soon after. The Chiefs had no answer for what the Hurricanes threw at them as Jordie Barrett got in on the tries, with Love doubling his tally after the hour-mark. Naitoa Ah Kuoi got one back for the Chiefs, which only ensured that the visitors didn’t end the final with a doughnut, but the champions would have the final say of the match, showpiece and the season with Jone Rova slamming down the exclamation mark on an incredible team performance. Hurricanes end decade-long Super Rugby title wait putting 60 points on Chiefs as All Blacks star Ruben Love dominates Undoubtedly a world-class player, Damian McKenzie produced one of his worst-ever performances in a Chiefs jersey with a truly horrendous first-half showing that hamstrung his team and gifted ascendancy to the Hurricanes time and time again. He butchered three restarts, threw a pass directly into Harkin’s clutches in a threatening attacking position, and was charged down a couple of times. After Moorby grabbed the opener, McKenzie gifted the hosts possession on the halfway line, slamming his restart into the in-goal with no pressure on Harkin, who forced it down for a scrum. Two minutes later, he made another error, missing touch with his penalty kick, again relieving pressure. Not too long after, the Hurricanes were in again through Love with the Chiefs under pressure in their own half. McKenzie further compounded his errors as right after Love’s try, he thumped the restart hard low, and the Hurricanes let it roll over the try line and for another scrum on halfway. With the Chiefs desperately looking to hit back, Norris tucks and carries in centre field, as does Dyer, stopped 18 metres out. McKenzie then drifted into space in the 35th minute but forced the attack and threw his pass straight to Harkin. Two minutes later, Harkin was in for the Canes’ next score, opening up a 26-0 lead. The ensuing restart, McKenzie attempted to go short, the wind caught it and gifted the Hurricanes a scrum again. There they won a penalty, and Love made it 29-0 at the break. Matters didn’t get much better for the All Blacks playmaker in the second half as he was held up in contact, with the Hurricanes awarded another scrum. Moorby doubled his tally after another lovely attacking move from the set-piece. In the 54th minute, McKenzie spilled the ball, undoing all his great cover work in the backfield, and the Hurricanes ruthlessly pounced with Barrett crossing the whitewash. Frankly, as good a player as McKenzie clearly is, tonight was not his night, and the mind boggles as to why the Chiefs’ coaching team did not act and put him out of his misery. Surely it couldn’t get much worse? In the words of Mick McCarthy: ‘It can!’ And it did. So often McKenzie has been the heart-beat, fulcrum of this team, but today he was a hindrance, a liability. Chiefs player ratings: Damian McKenzie produces final ‘horror show’ as several All Blacks stars endure ‘nightmare’ performances The 2009 Bulls. The 2012 Chiefs. The 1996 Blues. The 2018 Crusaders (or just about any of Scott Robertson’s teams). And now the 2026 Hurricanes have entered the conversation. The men from Wellington have waited 10 long years to add a second Super Rugby Pacific title and did so in a manner we have only seen a handful of times in this tournament’s history. Sure, they had their hiccups along the way, losing three regular season matches, but when it came to the crunch, the team that so often collapsed thrived, hammering the ACT Brumbies 66-12, a record score in Super Rugby knockouts. The Blues caused them a bit of trouble for 40 minutes in the semi-final, but once they started changing gears, they cruised to a 57-21 win. Then, they made it a hat-trick of 50+ point performances today with a mesmerizing showing where they completely outplayed the second-best team in the tournament. Tonight was the eighth occasion this season that ‘Canes racked up over 50 points in a match. The next best such tally this season? Four. The numbers behind their season are simply insane. They weren’t just the best points-scoring team during the regular season (562, including 86 tries), but they were also the most astute defence, conceding 298 points and 44 tries. Once they entered the knockout stages, the records continued to tumble, becoming the first team to score 100 tries in a single Super Rugby season, and they absolutely smashed their 2017 record of 97, finishing on 113! After crossing for nine tries in the final, the only issue Clark Laidlaw will have with the performance today was not keeping the Chiefs scoreless, but that won’t keep him sleepless at all as the ‘Canes claimed the biggest-ever Super Rugby final victory. Hurricanes player ratings: Jordie Barrett absolute ‘perfection’ as Ruben Love ‘decides’ All Blacks 10 battle while stunning wings break Super Rugby record New Zealand is never short on classy outside backs and wings in particular, but as Dave Rennie finalises his All Blacks squad ahead of Monday’s team announcement, two names surely have to feature: Fineanganofo and Moorby. The duo were sublime all season to break Joe Roff and Ben Lam’s try records and didn’t slip when it mattered most; in fact, during the play-off stages, they got even better. Moorby offers the benefit of being able to cover full-back too, which could be pivotal during the July Tests with Will Jordan sidelined, but considering how underwhelming the All Blacks’ wingers were as a collective last season, throwing uncapped players into the mix can’t be the worst idea. Fineanganofo’s situation is a bit trickier considering that he signed for the Newcastle Red Bulls before the start of the season, but selecting him in the squad should be non-negotiable. That can spark discussions around getting him out of that contract. The performances of Cam Roigard, Love, Barrett, Harkin, Billy Proctor and so many others made life easier for the free-scoring outside backs both today and throughout this season, but there is still so much value in having wingers who are in red-hot form and ruthlessly take opportunities that come their way. Where are they now? First Hurricanes team to win Super Rugby in 2016 After falling short of European glory with Leinster last season, Barrett was not going to let the opportunity to win the southern hemisphere’s premier club competition slip as he added a Super Rugby title to his URC winner’s medal from the last 12 months. The All Blacks midfield was otherworldly today, producing a nigh-on perfect performance in all facets of the game. He was yet again the ideal foil for Love in the number 12 jersey, taking on a lot of the playmaking duties, carrying strongly and seemingly always making the correct decision. He finished the game with 13 carries, 52 metres, five defenders beaten, four linebreaks, and pitched in with a try and an assist. Barrett was not alone, with Roigard and Love both producing arguably their best performances of the season, in stark contrast to their All Blacks teammate McKenzie on the other side of the pitch. Love claimed the man of the match award for his 25-point haul, which included two tries while he assisted another too. Roigard departed proceedings having controlled the insanely effective Hurricanes’ attack, throwing two try-assist passes but ultimately bossing the tempo from start to finish. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. Whilst the Hurricanes backs absolutely deserve the praise that will come their way, All Blacks assistant coaches Jason Ryan and Neil Barnes will be most pleased with what they saw up front. Hooker Asafo Aumua was a one-man wrecking ball once again and won his personal head-to-head with Chiefs star Samisoni Taukei’aho, despite both lineouts faltering at times. Aumua was also part of a ‘Canes pack that had the upper hand at scrum time, though wasn’t properly rewarded for their dominance, while Xavier Numia and Pasilio Tosi were extremely destructive in just about everything they did during their cameos. In the back-row, Flanders was superb in his final outing for the ‘Canes as were his partners in crime Du’Plessis Kirifi and Peter Lakai. The Hurricanes’ attack and backline brilliance stole the spotlight all season and again in the final but so much of their success was rooted in the performances in the forward pack, which certainly deserve their flowers. A team simply cannot score a record-breaking 114 tries in a season if the pack isn’t firing and firing on all cylinders and today, much like it has all season, the Hurricanes pack produced the goods. Furthermore, it wasn’t just the starters as the likes of Tyrel Lomax, Jacob Devery, Siale Lauaki and the first-ever double Hurricanes’ Super Rugby winner Brad Shields picked up from where the starters left off to complete the Chiefs’ embarrassment. title: Weekend’s hurling fixtures, throw-in times and TV details, including Clare v Dublin - The Irish Times
content: Clare v Dublin, Semple Stadium, Thurles, 7pm (Live on RTÉ 1) Clare and Dublin suffered multiple flesh wounds the last time we saw them. What matters now is how they have healed. In that process Clare hold the aces. It is easier to make excuses for their performance against Cork than for Dublin’s capitulation in the Leinster final. The pivotal game in Clare’s season so far had been eight days earlier against Tipperary and for a team with their age profile their mental and physical resources were simply depleted. Four weeks has allowed time for Mark Rodgers, Ryan Taylor and Darragh Lohan to recover from injuries and for everybody else to catch their breath. It is hackneyed to say that the Clare forward line is among the best in the championship, but the fact is they haven’t clicked since the opening game against Waterford. Shane O’Donnell and Peter Duggan have been below their best, David Reidy has been in and out, David Fitzgerald is a shadow of the player he was two years ago. Diarmuid Stritch and Seán Rynne are young players having a breakthrough season and they were terrific against Tipp; against Cork, though, they couldn’t swim against the tide. They weren’t alone. In Páirc Uí Chaoimh, Clare lost a game they didn’t need to win; it is impossible for Dublin to view the Leinster final in that way. In every respect they were wiped out. They coughed up 4-15 on turnovers, having only conceded 0-11 on turnovers to Kilkenny. Their shots output dropped from 45 to 32 from one game to the next. Against an elite opponent, those numbers are unsustainable. For all the strides that Dublin have made over the last 18 months, they lost the Leinster final in just the same way they have lost other Leinster finals over the last 13 years. For the sake of this group and their future together they can’t afford to implode again. Expect Clare to have straightened themselves out. Verdict: Clare Cork v Offaly, Semple Stadium, Thurles, 3.30pm (Live on RTÉ 1) Offaly’s re-emergence as a competitive force in the Leinster championship has been the most heartening story of the championship. The band of young players that reached three age-grade All-Ireland finals in as many years have more experience at senior level already than their peers in other counties and that is starting to tell. The question is how strong are form lines from the Leinster championship? Kilkenny and Wexford are at their lowest ebb in years and there are queries about Dublin against after the Leinster final. The unvarnished reality is that Cork are the strongest opponents they will have met so far. Cork have made four changes in their front eight, two of them enforced by injury. Brian Roche will not weaken Cork’s centrefield and Alan Walsh deserves his chance in the corner. Offaly took a beating in a challenge match against Clare recently and a similar fate awaits them here. title: Weekend’s football fixtures, throw-in times and TV details, including Armagh v Kerry and Dublin v Donegal - The Irish Times
content:
Subscribe to unlock this feature. Sign in or Subscribe Kerry v Armagh, Fitzgerald Stadium, 4pm (Live on GAA+) Seán O’Shea and Shane Ryan come back into contention for Kerry. They’re still missing Tom O’Sullivan but otherwise it looks like full steam ahead. Rory Grugan is back in the Armagh 26 but Blaine Hughes hasn’t recovered so Ethan Rafferty will be in goals. Kerry will target him, punching the bruise of last weekend’s killer mistake to see if they can rattle him, particularly at restart time. Kieran McGeeney would be happier if Hughes was available and if he still had Ben Crealey, and if Andrew Murnin had 70 minutes in him. Ultimately, Kerry’s wall of giants around the middle and their cutting edge up front might just shade it. Verdict: Kerry Both squads look fairly settled at this stage of the season, with Mattie Ruane the only notable addition to the Mayo 26. James Conlon really stood up on the scoring front for Meath against Derry but it’s hard not to think that Ruairí Kinsella’s absence will count against them at some point. Mayo’s recent home record is atrocious. They’ve lost four of their last five championship matches in Castlebar, with the only win coming against Sligo last summer. But their win over Monaghan is probably a slightly more impressive line on their CV than Meath’s over Derry, and they were good enough to bury Tyrone last week, if far from being clinical enough. A very tentative nod for Andy Moran’s side. Verdict: Mayo Down were already well-fancied favourites for this competition and now they have Pat Havern back. But they are far from infallible, as evidenced by the sound beating Offaly gave them at the end of May. Fermanagh haven’t beaten Down in the championship since 2009 but they’ve put together an impressive Tailteann run this time around, twice beating Division Three opposition in Sligo and Wexford. They went out in the semi-final to Kildare this time last year and anything other than the same fate here would be a surprise. Verdict: Down Offaly v Wicklow, Croke Park, 5pm (Live on RTÉ News) After a very difficult league campaign, Offaly look to have finally rediscovered their mojo. The Faithful County lost all seven Division Two games and were dumped out of Leinster by Laois in the opening round. But they have got to the semi-final stages of the Tailteann Cup with impressive victories over Clare, Down and Wexford – three teams with their own title-winning credentials at the outset of this competition. Jack Bryant looked dangerous against Wexford, scoring 1-3. Dean Healy and Mark Jackson were central to Wicklow’s win over Antrim last time out, but the Garden County haven’t been as consistent as Offaly in recent weeks. Verdict: Offaly Dublin v Donegal, Croke Park, 1.15pm (Live on RTÉ 1) The Neller or Nowhere campaign faded out quickly but for Dublin and Donegal there’s no doubt this fixture arrives with a dollop of Now or Never. There are no more safety nets left. Donegal’s form is difficult to fully break down – losing to both Down and Cork at home in recent weeks has to be a worry for Jim McGuinness. Donegal’s energy levels and intent were really low against Cork last weekend. What happened to the team that stormed Killarney? The hurdle of Dublin might just be the ideal challenge for Donegal right now, though. The Dubs will also frame this fixture as a chance to kick-start their season. Con O’Callaghan’s return has been significant but one wonders if enough players in the Dublin dressingroom actually believe they can go all the way to an All-Ireland final this year. Donegal don’t have that problem. Verdict: Donegal Monaghan v Westmeath, St Tiarnach’s Park, Clones, 4pm (Live on GAA+) It has been a great season for Westmeath but some of the soundbites in the immediate aftermath of their loss to Galway last weekend indicated the demands of the last few weeks might be starting to catch up with the squad. Monaghan have had a demanding season too – and both sides have had their fair share of injury setbacks. But Gabriel Bannigan’s side enter this game with the momentum of last week’s win over Roscommon driving them on. Their experienced players like Jack McCarron, Dessie Ward and Conor McCarthy were central to that win against the Rossies. Monaghan looked renergised. In what is likely to be a close contest, that extra bit of desire and determination might prove to be the difference. title: Pine64 Pinevoice – A $50 RISC-V Smart Speaker for Home Assistant based on Bouffalo Lab BL606P MCU - CNX Software
content: Reviews, tutorials and the latest news about embedded systems, IoT, open-source hardware, SBC's, microcontrollers, processors, and more After over two years in the making, Pine64 has now launched the PineVoice (previously PineVox) smart speaker based on the Bouffalo Lab BL606P RISC-V wireless microcontroller with WiFi, Bluetooth, and Zigbee radio interfaces. The device also features two microphones, a speaker, a USB 2.0 OTG port, volume buttons, a mute button with LED, a start/stop button, and four RGB LEDs. The PineVoice smart speaker is mainly designed to work with Home Assistant. The default firmware supports Wyoming Satellite protocol, which, according to the project itself, is now deprecated, and the ESPHome protocol is now preferred. The documentation includes more technical details with PDF schematics for the main and bottom boards, and software resources with links to various repositories for the SDK and firmware development. However, I can’t find the default firmware’s source code for now since there’s nothing specific to the PineVoice. Pine64 explains that the PineVoice is still in early-stage development and may experience performance issues, notably for wake word detection. It should probably be considered as a smart speaker devkit, rather than a consumer device for your Home Assistant setup. This may change in the future if the firmware improves. With that in mind, if you’d like to go ahead, the PineVoice can be purchased for $49.99 on the Pine64 store. It ships with a USB-A to USB-C cable and a Quick Start Guide. Warranty is valid for 30 days. title: Leinster v Bulls: Five takeaways as 'not a shred' of Springboks' World Cup-winning pedigree evident against Irish giants who 'ruthlessly' charge to URC title - Planet Rugby
content: Leinster wing James Lowe against Bulls in URC Final. Following Leinster’s 36-7 United Rugby Championship (URC) Grand Final victory over the Bulls, here are our five takeaways from the clash at Croke Park in Dublin. Leinster are champions of the United Rugby Championship for a second season running, the first side to go back-to-back in the competition’s history, and they did it with a performance of such cold control that the trophy was as good as won inside half an hour. The 36-7 scoreline reads like a massacre, and in the opening moments that decided it, it pretty much was, as the Bulls did everything in their power to hand the game to Leinster. What buried them was not domination but their own generosity, and the ruthlessness of a Leinster outfit that took every gift and asked for more. Same venue as last June, same opponent, very nearly the same story, played out this time in front of a thin Friday-night crowd of around 40,000 in a stadium built for 82,000, the Bulls came to Croke Park for a fourth final and left with a fourth defeat. The tone was set inside the opening exchanges. Tommy O’Brien went the length after Handre Pollard spilled possession in his own half, a score born of Jacques Nienaber’s blitz defence flying off the line and forcing the error. Rieko Ioane followed, then Jack Conan from the maul, and the Bulls, who had emptied the tank in that astonishing Murrayfield comeback a fortnight ago, looked for all the world like a team that had played its final the week before. To add insult to injury, yellow cards for Canan Moodie and Willie le Roux left the visitors with 14 on the pitch for half of that critical first half. Sam Prendergast masterclass leads Leinster to thumping URC title success over disappointing Bulls The contest was billed as a coronation of experience at fly-half. Pollard, 81 Test caps and two World Cups, against Sam Prendergast, the 23-year-old whose selection ahead of Ciarán Frawley had half of Ireland arguing all week. Yet it ran the opposite way to the script from the first whistle, with the young Irishman producing the match of his career thus far. Prendergast saved a certain Bulls try by falling on a loose ball with Stravino Jacobs bearing down, kicked four of his five conversions and a penalty, and finished a try of his own making after hanging a high ball into the Bulls 22 that not a single player in green and white, Le Roux included, bothered to chase. Bulls player ratings: Handre Pollard drops an ‘absolute mare’, departing Springbok ‘robbed’ as World Cup winners outplayed in ’embarrassing’ URC Final defeat He walked off with the Player of the Match award, the most pointed answer imaginable to a fortnight of questions. Pollard, by contrast, had an absolute nightmare by his lofty standards on the pitch, his evening summed up by a first-half penalty kicked clean over the dead-ball line. The young man with the doubts over his head played like the seasoned head, and the seasoned world champion head played like the doubt. By the time Harry Byrne came off the bench to score Leinster’s fifth, the gulf at fly-half had become its own running commentary on the night. If the ten channel was a mismatch, the nine channel was a masterclass. Jamison Gibson-Park dictated tempo, territory and tone, the conductor of everything good Leinster did, and he handed his fly-half the smoothest of evenings. His quick thinking made the Ioane try, a darting ball to the middle of the pitch that put Hugo Keenan through a hole nobody filled before a sublime pass sent the departing centre over. Across from him, Embrose Papier, the URC’s own Player of the Season, was anonymous and poor. The Bulls had clearly come to play in the air, Papier peppering the Dublin sky with contestables, and the aerial battle finished 16-4 to Leinster. Keenan claimed everything that came down, the full-back also topping the match for running metres on 75, defenders beaten on eight, and clean breaks on three, a complete attacking display from the back. The Player of the Season kicked into a contest his side won four times in eighty minutes, and kept kicking long after the lesson was obvious. Twice Moodie did finally climb highest, and twice he tapped the ball straight into Leinster hands, first Max Deegan, then James Ryan. It was a complete abdication of one of the critical areas for the Bulls. Leinster player ratings: Sam Prendergast’s ‘rehabilitation’ and ‘proper nuisance’ forwards catch the eye in ’emphatic’ culling of the Bulls There is no kinder way to frame what the Bulls did to themselves. Three deliberate knock-ons brought three yellow cards, two of them Bulls in Moodie and Le Roux, and Leinster plundered the bulk of their points while Pretoria were short-handed. Referee Andrea Piardi was consistent to the letter, the night’s only officiating blemish coming from the TMO box, where the Bulls had two scores denied, the first a marginal call you would not want to lose a final on. The lineout fell apart, picked clean by Max Deegan, whose two steals and two turnovers were the chief reason the set-piece never functioned. Springboks legend hits out at URC Final officials for fabricating ‘fiction’ in Bulls’ disallowed tries A clever, streetwise side froze on the one stage where all that Springbok nous was meant to count. 11 of their starting XV were capped Springboks, Le Roux a centurion, Pollard a double World Cup winner, and not a shred of that pedigree showed when the prize was biggest. Four finals without a win has stopped being misfortune and become a pattern. There is a hard law out on the highveld; when the old bulls can no longer hold the herd, they are culled, and a herd led by Le Roux at 36 and Pollard carrying the miles of two World Cups was overrun by a younger, hungrier one in Leinster blue. Credit, though, where it is owed. Marcell Coetzee, 23 tackles and 11 carries, and Ruan Nortje, the game’s top tackler on 24, fronted up to the last, and the scrum was the one platform Pretoria genuinely won. A dominant scrum counts for little, mind, when the discipline, the lineout and the aerial game are all leaking at once. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. For a clutch of Leinster men, this was goodbye. James Lowe signed off his 102nd and final appearance before Tokyo Sungoliath, the emotion of the night dented only by a yellow card of his own for a deliberate knock-on. Ioane marked his last act in blue with a farewell try before heading home to the Blues, while Luke McGrath leaves for Perpignan, Jerry Cahir for Connacht, and Frawley, also Connacht-bound, had already played his last. Caelan Doris, forced off on six minutes with a foot injury, will spend an anxious few days before Ireland’s summer tour, though Conan’s arrival and a fourth try in his fourth separate Grand Final softened the blow. The lasting story, though, belongs to Leo Cullen. His side have not won the Champions Cup since 2018, and the wounds of the Bilbao humiliation against Bordeaux-Bègles were still raw. He answered in the only currency that silences a press box. Back-to-back URC titles, a record-flavoured night for a club that demands silverware, and a coach who walks into the summer with the job and the doubters both settled. title: USA v Australia referee Felix Zwayer pulls up with cramp towards end of World Cup match - Yahoo Sports
content: Experienced World Cup referee Felix Zwayer pulled up with cramp towards the end of the USA’s win over Australia in Seattle. The German official, 45, required help from both the USA’s Folarin Balogun and Australia's Aiden O'Neill, who stretched out his left leg after Zwayer fell to the turf. Zwayer had just brandished a flurry of yellow cards at the end of what was a dominant victory for the USA at Lumen Field. With just a couple of minutes of stoppage time remaining, Zwayer also required an energy gel - which was rushed onto the pitch by fourth official Katia Garcia. Zwayer was able to get to his feet and see out the rest of the match, with the USA beating Australia 2-0 to reach the knockout stages. The USA’s match against Australia started at noon local time in Seattle, with temperatures towards the end of the Group D clash reached around 26 degrees with 45 per cent humidity. Every match at this 48-team World Cup is controversially featuring hydration breaks at the midway point of each half, allowing players to take on additional fluids. It’s not unusual to see players suffer cramp towards the end of matches taking place in heat, while referees have to cover a lot of ground to keep up with play. Zwayer is one of Europe’s top referees and took charge of the Euro 2024 semi-final between England and the Netherlands as well as the 2025 Europa League final between Manchester United and Tottenham.

title: World Cup 2026: Bukayo Saka unlikely to start for England v Ghana - BBC
content: Bukayo Saka came on in the 72nd minute of England's opening win against Croatia England head coach Thomas Tuchel has hinted that Bukayo Saka is unlikely to be in contention to start against Ghana on Tuesday. Saka came off the bench in the 4-2 World Cup win over Croatia on Wednesday, and immediately provided an assist to fellow substitute Marcus Rashford, who slotted home England's fourth. Before the tournament, Tuchel said Saka would require managing through the opening stages because of what is understood to be an Achilles tendinitis issue. On Monday, Saka insisted he was ready to play and was prepared to "gamble" on his fitness to help the team during the World Cup. However, Tuchel says the Arsenal attacker is unlikely to start until the final group game against Panama in New Jersey on 27 June. He said: "Bukayo is ready and will get more and more ready. I think once we go to the last game of this group he will be ready." Saka has been carrying the issue for some time, and while there was concern behind the scenes at Arsenal about the niggle they deemed their forward fit enough to start regularly during their triumphant title run-in. It is understood that Saka's ongoing Achilles issue has not deteriorated since the climax of the domestic season. Arsenal boss Mikel Arteta, who is often very guarded with regards to his players' injury concerns, has generally kept information about Saka's condition in-house but Tuchel's admission that the 24-year-old has to be managed through at least part of the World Cup has thrust the winger's fitness into the limelight. Tuchel's latest comments appear to show that the German is protecting Saka, knowing the attacker will likely be a crucial asset during the latter stages of the tournament - but could also start the game against Ghana if required. title: Fernando Mendoza versus Iowa, Part V of Las Vegas Raiders’ Mendoza Mania - Silver And Black Pride
content: We’re onto Week 5 in Silver and Black Pride’s Mendoza Mania series, providing film breakdowns on every game from the Las Vegas Raiders’ No. 1 pick of the 2026 NFL Draft, Fernando Mendoza’s last season at Indiana. The theme of this matchup against Iowa was pressure. The stakes were high for the Hoosiers, as they were on the road to take on a conference opponent that finished the season as a ranked team. And the Hawkeyes gave them just about all they could handle, with Indiana squeaking out a 20-15 victory. Add Silver And Black Pride as a preferred source to see more of our reporting on Google. Iowa was bringing the heat with blitz after blitz throughout the contest, and Mendoza was under pressure on 12 out of 30 dropbacks (40 percent), according to Pro Football Focus. That led to an underwhelming stat line with 13 completions on 23 attempts (56.5 percent) for 233 yards, a touchdown and his first interception of the season, as we’ll get a look at how he struggled and succeeded to handle the pressure. We’ll start with a couple of negative plays to end on a high note, and pocket management was one of Mendoza’s biggest areas of improvement from this game. Here, Indiana is running a mesh concept, and they get the coverage they were hoping for with Iowa blitzing a linebacker, taking the low hole defender out of the play call while the coverage unit runs Cover 1. With the defense playing man-to-man, the cornerback has to adjust his path to avoid getting picked, leaving Elijah Sarratt wide open with room to run for a first down or more on the short drag route. However, the right tackle gets beaten around the edge pretty quickly, so the pressure is coming. Mendoza clearly feels it, as he takes a step up in the pocket. However, he starts to move laterally instead of taking one more step up and dumping the ball to Sarratt. That makes the edge-rusher’s job a little easier because it closes the gap between him and the quarterback, and this nearly ends up being a strip sack. Luckily, the ball just falls incomplete. But it is third down, so this play still leads to a change of possession. What makes it more frustrating is that this could have set up a scoring opportunity had Mendoza stepped up in the pocket a little more instead of drifting into the pressure. To be honest, this is a tough one for the quarterback because Iowa wins this rep in the huddle with the perfect play call for what Indiana has dialed up. Pre-snap, the Hawyekes show blitz with one linebacker walked up on the line of scrimmage and the other backer, along with the two safeties, creeping toward the line of scrimmage. On top of that, the safeties have good timing where they come downhill shortly before the snap and before the offense can make an adjustment, audible or alert a hot route. So, it’s a six-man pressure where both safeties blitz, but the protection scheme has to account for the middle linebacker since he’s also a blitz threat. That means the defense’s call functions similarly to a seven-man pressure, where there’s going to be a free rusher since the center has to make sure the linebacker isn’t coming before he can help pick up the unblocked defender. Meanwhile, Indiana has its three receivers run deeper routes since it’s third and 12. There is a checkdown option built into the play that can help beat the blitz with the tight end running a quick out route. However, the Hawkeyes had the perfect answer for that, with the other linebacker who was on the line of scrimmage playing press man coverage against the tight end. As a result, Mendoza doesn’t have anyone open to get the ball out quickly, and the unblocked safety is coming, in addition to the other safety who beats the running back in pass protection. It feels like Mendoza starts to panic in the pocket, throwing off his back foot and forcing the ball to Omar Cooper Jr. The pass ends up sailing over Cooper’s head and into the defensive back’s hands for a late-game interception that almost cost Indiana the win. Again, the offense gets beaten by the play call, so there isn’t much the quarterback can do to turn this into a positive play. But this is a situation where you’d like to see him try to create/make a play out of structure, or just take the sack. The latter isn’t ideal on third down, but it’s better than a pick in a tie game that gives the other team the ball in scoring territory with less than three minutes left. But part of why the National Champs ended up raising a trophy at the end of the campaign is that their play-callers and quarterback were great at making adjustments. To be fair, they did have some luck on their side to have a second chance at a game-winning drive since the Hawkeyes missed the field goal after the pick. But the Hoosiers made the most of their opportunity. This is almost the same situation as the last clip, with the offense facing a third and long at midfield while the defense brings the house with both safeties blitzing. They also send the linebacker to bring even more heat. However, the offense is ready for it this time. Indiana runs a three-man route, where the running back and the tight end are involved in the protection scheme instead of just the back. That negates the linebacker who took away the tight end last time, as that backer ends up covering grass, while the offense has more bodies to pick up the blitz. Meanwhile, Sarratt, the single receiver at the top of the screen, runs a slant against off-coverage to be the quick-hitting answer against the pressure. So, Mendoza can get rid of the ball right after taking the snap, and he does a great job of stepping into the throw as the pocket is collapsing to hit Sarratt in stride, who breaks one tackle and has nothing but green grass in front of him to take it to the house for the win. The throw here isn’t much to speak of, and of course, Mendoza gets some help from the coaching staff with the improved play call. Regardless, this is a great in-game adjustment by both parties and encouraging to see from the No. 1 pick since he’s already managing the pocket better. As a preview for the next game/breakdown, he was a lot better when it came to handling pressure against Oregon just two weeks and one game later. For clarity, these last three clips aren’t in sequential order, meaning they’re jumping around from different points in the game. On this one, we’ll get an even better example of Mendoza handling pressure in the pocket much more soundly than what was previously seen. Iowa blitzes its two linebackers while the right edge defender drops into coverage to execute a three-deep, three-under fire zone. But Indiana has a perfect play call for it by putting the corner at the top of the screen in conflict. The corner’s first read is the man he’s lined up across from, but he’s ultimately responsible for whichever receiver runs a deep route between the two that are on his side of the field. With the outside receiver (who is actually a tight end) running a short curl and the slot receiver running seam, the corner has to pick up the seam route but is late to it since he was lined up across from the short curl. Especially with the defense trying to disguise the coverage pre-snap by the field safety showing a two-deep coverage before rolling down and the boundary safety all the way on the other hashmark, the slot receiver is open for an explosive play. However, the Hawkeyes also have a twist going on with the blitzing linebackers, and the running back doesn’t pick up on it while the left guard has to pass off the defensive tackle to the left tackle, allowing a free rusher right through the A-gap. But Mendoza stays calm under pressure this time and delivers a perfect pass to the seam route while taking a hit, allowing the offense to beat the blitz and capitalize with an explosive play. Now, we’re going back to the game-winning drive, and the clip above set up the slant to Sarratt for the touchdown that broke the tie and gave Indiana the victory. There is no blitz or pressure this time, as the Hawkeyes show a two-high look pre-snap and roll into Cover 1 post-snap. Once Mendoza sees the safeties rotate, he knows he has a one-on-one opportunity with Sarratt on a go route against a corner in man coverage. Granted, the corner has pretty good coverage where he stays on top of the receiver and doesn’t allow any separation. So, the quarterback throws the receiver open by hitting a back-shoulder pass, which those two became famous for last season. The ball is perfectly placed and thrown with good velocity, going from the far hashmarks to outside the numbers, to beat the coverage and put Indiana in Iowa’s territory. Three plays later, Mendoza and Sarratt connected on the slant for the win. We’re going to end toward the beginning, as this play came in the second quarter and was the best throw Mendoza made in the game. Technically, it doesn’t quite fit with the overall theme of pressure since he doesn’t get hit or anything like that. But Iowa does dial up a blitz with the three-deep, three-under fire zone behind it. With this play-call, the cornerback at the bottom of the screen is supposed to take away or stay on top of a deep route from the outside receiver. However, the corner plays it poorly by not working for enough depth. Mendoza recognizes that and sees the safety is on the hashmark with his hips pointed toward the line of scrimmage. That’s going to make it almost impossible for the safety to get to the sideline in time to break up the pass, so the quarterback lets it rip to the go route for what essentially becomes a hole shot between the two defenders. This throw really highlights the Heisman Trophy winner’s arm strength as it’s on a line from the far hash to the opposite sideline and over 30 yards down the field, on top of being into the wind and beating the defensive backs. That’s an excellent read and one hell of a throw to flip the field. title: France XV v England XV: Five takeaways as Benhard Janse van Rensburg blows 'golden chance' - Planet Rugby
content: France XV celebrate a try against England XV. Following France’s emphatic 35-19 win over England in their non-cap friendly in Vannes, here are our takeaways from a sun-drenched Stade de la Rabine. Benhard Janse van Rensburg blew a golden chance to mark his first appearance for his adopted country with a try as England’s dreadful start to 2026 continued in Brittany. Two days before Steve Borthwick names his squad for the inaugural Nations Championship, a team of predominantly fringe players was well beaten by a more cohesive France XV in this non-cap clash. Borthwick hoped victory at Stade de la Rabine would help turn the page on the country’s worst ever Six Nations campaign. Instead, an error-strewn performance reminded him how much work there is to do. Van Rensburg‘s contribution rather summed up the evening for the visitors. Off the bench and desperate to impress on his first appearance wearing the rose, the South African ran onto a George Ford pass only needing to catch the ball to score – and spilled it. Three months after coming within seconds of beating France in the Six Nations, England were no match for Les Bleus on the Brittany coast. For context, they selected only three of the 23 that played in Paris, Seb Atkinson, Caden Murley and Marcus Smith. Whereas France, benefiting from Bordeaux’s shock failure to make the Top-14 playoffs, had a large number of European champions to call upon. Yet so much of England’s failing was self-inflicted. Harry Randall and Smith each kicked out on the full, lineouts were stolen or not thrown straight, too many balls to count went to ground. England XV player ratings: Cadan Murley ‘pushes his case’ for Springboks Test as Noah Caluori ‘not out of place’ But it was when the benches were cleared that the real pain began. England’s scrum was no match for the power coming at them. They became so discombobulated that their concentration went as well. With a minute to go every England player had his back turned as Baptiste Jauneau took a quick tap-and-go and linked with Fabien Brau-Boirie, who sauntered clear untouched for France’s fifth try. Well, England scored with their opening attack when Murley finished off a sweeping right-to-left move, fending off Theo Attissogbe to touch down in the corner. They also ended the half with a tidy try after Noah Caluori was sent up the middle and fed Smith, who stepped inside the full-back to score. There was the welcome sight of George Martin, now of Saracens, back in an England shirt for the first time since February 2025. Tom Curry also enjoyed game time for the first time since finally recovering from the grade 3 calf tear that had sidelined him since early March. Asher Opoku-Fordjour proved he can hold up a scrum on the loosehead and Max Ojomoh returned to England colours for the first time since his player of the match display against Argentina in the autumn and marked the occasion with a last-minute try. That, however, is about the size of it. The big hope, from an English point of view, was that Caluori would transfer the brilliance of his debut club season onto the international stage. Only one player in Gallagher PREM history has scored more tries in a season than the 19-year old’s 18 in 13 matches this term, Exeter number eight Sam Simmonds in season 2020/21. Why Northampton must follow Harry Kane and England’s lead as Saints legend reveals the ‘secret’ to winning finals Could he take that deadly finishing and become a lethal weapon on the international scene? Could all those fans clamouring for him to be thrown into the Nations Championship mix have their prayers answered. The first thing to say is he let nobody down. He leapt high to claim a restart, twice came off his wing to assist with tries. He chased, he tackled and he thought he had scored himself after beating France on the outside and haring clear. Unfortunately, the 53rd minute score was chalked off because Jamie Blamire, newly arrived from the bench, knocked on in the build up. His time will undoubtedly come. But right now, does he get in on the wing ahead of Immanuel Feyi-Waboso, Tommy Freeman and Tom Roebuck? No he doesn’t. Is he right there alongside Murley and Henry Arundell? Absolutely. Throwing him in against South Africa at Ellis Park would be unfair. Giving him a start off the bench against Fiji makes more sense. A year ago England made a dog’s dinner of this fixture at Twickenham. They led by 12 points with five minutes left and found a way to lose, allowing Romain Taofifénua to score the winner two minutes after the clock entered the red. Want more from Planet Rugby? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for world-class coverage you can trust. What harm did it do to their summer? None at all, as it happened. Ford and Jamie George pulled a squad together missing 13 Lions and led them on an unbeaten tour of the Americas; beating Argentina, twice, and the United States. The difference this time is the quality of the opposition is far higher. The Springboks are on a different level to the rest at the moment. England then face the logistical challenge of flying back to Liverpool for another hugely physical encounter (against Fiji), before boarding another long haul flight to Argentina. The worry is they have no momentum and confidence, whatever anyone says, cannot be high. Borthwick could desperately do with tapping into the buccaneering belief of his Northampton players and the never-say-die spirit of Exeter lads like Henry Slade and Feyi-Waboso.
